paragraphs: Alyosha helped Father Zossima into his bedroom and sat him down on the bed. It was a small room with only the bare necessities. There was a narrow iron bedstead with a strip of felt for a mattress. In the corner, under the ikons, stood a reading-desk with a cross and the Gospel lying on it. The elder sank down on the bed, exhausted. His eyes glittered and he breathed hard. He looked at Alyosha intently, as though weighing something.
“Go, my dear boy, go. Porfiry is enough for me. Hurry, you are needed there. Go and wait at the Father Superior’s table.”
“Let me stay here,” Alyosha begged.

“You are needed more there. There is no peace there. You will wait on them and be of use. If evil spirits rise up, say a prayer. And remember, my son”—the elder liked to call him that—“this is not the place for you in the future. When it is God’s will to call me, leave the monastery. Go away for good.”
Alyosha started.

“What is it? This is not your place for the time being. I bless you for great service in the world. Yours will be a long pilgrimage. And you will have to take a wife, too. You will have to bear _all_ before you come back. There will be much to do. But I do not doubt you, and so I send you out. Christ is with you. Do not abandon Him, and He will not abandon you. You will see great sorrow, and in that sorrow you will be happy. This is my last message to you: in sorrow, seek happiness. Work, work without ceasing. Remember my words, for although I will talk with you again, not only my days but my hours are numbered.”
Alyosha’s face again showed strong emotion. The corners of his mouth quivered.

“What is it now?” Father Zossima asked, smiling gently. “The people of the world follow their dead with tears, but here we rejoice over the father who is departing. We rejoice and pray for him. Leave me, I must pray. Go, and hurry. Stay close to your brothers. And not to one of them only, but to both.”

Father Zossima raised his hand to bless him. Alyosha could not protest, though he longed very much to stay. He longed, too, to ask what the elder’s bowing to Dmitri meant. The question was on the tip of his tongue, but he did not dare ask it. He knew the elder would have explained it unasked if he had thought it right. But plainly it was not his will. That action had made a terrible impression on Alyosha; he believed blindly in its mysterious meaning. Mysterious, and perhaps awful.

As he hurried out of the hermitage grounds to reach the monastery in time to serve at the Father Superior’s dinner, he felt a sudden pang at his heart and stopped short. He seemed to hear Father Zossima’s words again, foretelling his approaching end. What the elder had foretold so exactly must surely come to pass. Alyosha believed that without question. But how could he be left without him? How could he live without seeing and hearing him? Where would he go? The elder had told him not to weep, and to leave the monastery. Good God! It was a long time since Alyosha had felt such anguish. He hurried through the copse that lay between the hermitage and the monastery. Unable to bear the weight of his thoughts, he gazed at the ancient pines beside the path. He did not have far to go—about five hundred paces. He expected to meet no one at that hour, but at the first turn of the path he saw Rakitin. Rakitin was waiting for someone.
“Are you waiting for me?” asked Alyosha, catching up with him.

“Yes,” grinned Rakitin. “You’re hurrying to the Father Superior’s, I know. He’s giving a banquet. There hasn’t been a banquet like it since the Superior entertained the Bishop and General Pahatov, remember? I won’t be there, but you go and hand round the sauces. Tell me one thing, Alexey: what does that vision mean? That’s what I want to ask you.”
“What vision?”
“That bowing to your brother Dmitri. And didn’t he knock the ground with his forehead, too!”
“You mean Father Zossima?”
“Yes, Father Zossima.”
“Knocked the ground?”
“Ah, a disrespectful expression! Well, so what? Anyway, what does that vision mean?”
“I don’t know what it means, Misha.”

“I knew he wouldn’t explain it to you! There’s nothing wonderful about it, of course, just the usual holy mummery. But the performance had a purpose. All the pious people in town will talk about it and spread the story through the province, wondering what it meant. To my mind the old man really has a keen nose; he sniffed out a crime. Your house stinks of it.”
“What crime?”
Rakitin plainly had something he was eager to talk about.

“It’ll happen in your family, this crime. Between your brothers and your rich old father. So Father Zossima flopped down to be ready for whatever turns up. If something happens later, it’ll be: ‘Ah, the holy man foresaw it, he prophesied it!’ Though it’s a poor sort of prophecy, flopping down like that. ‘Ah, but it was symbolic,’ they’ll say, ‘an allegory,’ and the devil knows what else! It’ll be remembered to his glory: ‘He predicted the crime and marked the criminal!’ That’s always the way with these crazy fanatics; they cross themselves at the tavern and throw stones at the temple. Your elder’s the same: he takes a stick to a just man and falls at the feet of a murderer.”
“What crime? What murderer? What do you mean?”
Alyosha stopped dead. Rakitin stopped, too.

“What murderer? As if you didn’t know! I’ll bet you’ve thought of it before. That’s interesting, too, by the way. Listen, Alyosha, you always tell the truth, though you always sit between two stools. Have you thought of it or not? Answer.”
“I have,” answered Alyosha in a low voice. Even Rakitin was taken aback.
“What? Have you really?” he cried.
“I ... I haven’t exactly thought it,” muttered Alyosha, “but the moment you began speaking so strangely, I felt I had thought of it myself.”
“You see? (And how well you put it!) Looking at your father and your brother Mitya today, you thought of a crime. So I’m not mistaken?”
“But wait, wait a minute,” Alyosha broke in uneasily. “What has made you see all this? Why does it interest you? That’s the first question.”

“Two questions, unconnected but natural. I’ll take them separately. What made me see it? I wouldn’t have seen it if I hadn’t suddenly understood your brother Dmitri, seen right into the heart of him all at once. I grasped the whole man from one trait. These very honest but passionate people have a line that mustn’t be crossed. If it were, he’d go for your father with a knife. But your father’s a drunken, shameless old sinner who can never draw the line—if they both let themselves go, they’ll both come to grief.”
“No, Misha, no. If that’s all, you’ve reassured me. It won’t come to that.”

“But why are you trembling? Let me tell you: he may be honest, our Mitya (he’s stupid, but honest), but he’s a sensualist. That’s the very definition and inner core of him. It’s your father who handed down his low sensuality to him. Do you know, I simply wonder at you, Alyosha, how you’ve managed to stay pure. You’re a Karamazov too, you know! In your family sensuality is carried to the point of disease. But now these three sensualists are watching one another with knives in their belts. The three of them are knocking heads together, and you may be the fourth.”
“You’re wrong about that woman. Dmitri—despises her,” said Alyosha, with a sort of shudder.

“Grushenka? No, brother, he doesn’t despise her. He has openly abandoned his betrothed for her, so he doesn’t despise her. There’s something here, my dear boy, that you don’t understand yet. A man will fall in love with some beauty, with a woman’s body, or even with a part of a woman’s body (a sensualist can understand that), and he’ll abandon his own children for her, sell his father and mother and his country, Russia, too. If he’s honest, he’ll steal; if he’s humane, he’ll murder; if he’s faithful, he’ll deceive. Pushkin, the poet of women’s feet, sang about their feet in his verse. Others don’t sing their praises, but they can’t look at a woman’s feet without a thrill—and it’s not only the feet. Contempt is no help here, brother, even if he did despise Grushenka. He does, but he can’t tear himself away.”
“I understand that,” Alyosha jerked out suddenly.

“Really? Well, I suppose you do understand, since you blurt it out at the first word,” said Rakitin, spitefully. “That escaped you without your meaning it, and the confession’s all the more precious. So it’s a familiar subject; you’ve thought about it already, about sensuality, I mean! Oh, you virgin soul! You’re a quiet one, Alyosha, you’re a saint, I know, but the devil only knows what you’ve thought about, and what you know already! You’re pure, but you’ve been down into the depths.... I’ve been watching you for a long time. You’re a Karamazov yourself; you’re a thorough Karamazov—no doubt birth and selection have something to answer for. You’re a sensualist from your father, a crazy saint from your mother. Why are you trembling? So it’s true? Do you know, Grushenka has been begging me to bring you along. ‘I’ll pull off his cassock,’ she says. You can’t imagine how she keeps begging me to bring you. I wondered why she took such an interest in you. Do you know, she’s an extraordinary woman, too!”
“Thank her and say I’m not coming,” said Alyosha, with a strained smile. “Finish what you were saying, Misha. I’ll tell you my idea afterward.”

“There’s nothing to finish. It’s all clear. It’s the same old tune, brother. If even you are a sensualist at heart, what about your brother Ivan? He’s a Karamazov, too. What lies at the root of all you Karamazovs is that you’re all sensual, grasping and crazy! Your brother Ivan writes theological articles as a joke, for some idiotic motive of his own that nobody knows, though he’s an atheist, and he admits himself it’s a fraud—that’s your brother Ivan. He’s trying to get Mitya’s betrothed for himself, and I think he’ll succeed, too. What’s more, it’ll be with Mitya’s consent. Mitya will hand his betrothed over to him to be rid of her and escape to Grushenka. And he’s ready to do that in spite of all his nobility and unselfishness. Mark that. Those are the most fatal people! Who the devil can make you out? He knows how vile he is and goes on with it! Let me tell you, too, that the old man, your father, is standing in Mitya’s way now. He has suddenly gone crazy over Grushenka. His mouth waters at the sight of her. It’s simply on her account that he made that scene in the cell just now, simply because Miüsov called her an ‘abandoned creature.’ He’s worse than a tom-cat in love. At first she was only employed by him in connection with his taverns and some other shady business, but now he has suddenly realized what she is and has gone wild about her. He keeps pestering her with his offers, not honorable ones, of course. And they’ll collide, the precious father and son, on that path! But Grushenka favors neither of them; she’s still playing with them and teasing them both, working out which she can get more out of. For though she could filch a lot of money from the papa, he wouldn’t marry her, and maybe he’ll turn stingy in the end and keep his purse shut. That’s where Mitya’s value comes in: he has no money, but he’s ready to marry her. Yes, ready to marry her! To abandon his betrothed, a rare beauty, Katerina Ivanovna, who’s rich and the daughter of a colonel, and to marry Grushenka, who has been the mistress of a dissolute old merchant, Samsonov, a coarse, uneducated, provincial mayor. Some murderous conflict may well come out of all this, and that’s what your brother Ivan is waiting for. It would suit him down to the ground. He’ll carry off Katerina Ivanovna, for whom he’s languishing, and pocket her dowry of sixty thousand. That’s very alluring to start with, for a nobody and a beggar. And note that he won’t be wronging Mitya, but doing him the greatest service. For I know for a fact that only last week Mitya, drunk in a tavern with some gypsy girls, cried out aloud that he was unworthy of his betrothed, Katya, but that his brother Ivan was the man who deserved her. And Katerina Ivanovna won’t in the end refuse such a fascinating man as Ivan. She’s hesitating between the two of them already. And how has that Ivan won you all over, so that you all worship him? He’s laughing at you, and enjoying himself at your expense.”
